title: Silent Implementation Shortfall in LLM-Written Trading Code
abstract: Traders increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to turn a strategy described in desk language into executable code. We measure the cost of that translation. Holding the strategy, the price path and the frictions fixed, we compare a reference implementation with the implementation an LLM writes from the same description; the return difference is an implementation shortfall attributable to translation alone, with the strategy’s own alpha differenced away. Across equity index and cryptocurrency markets, most programs written by low-cost models run without error yet depart from the authorised behaviour, and the median absolute shortfall ranges from several hundred to over two thousand basis points of initial equity. The sign of the average shortfall varies across models and samples, so the loss is better described as unpredictable deviation than as a haircut. The shortfall is larger for strategies whose risk logic carries state for longer, but this gradient is explained by holding duration: within a given type of risk control, models do not diverge more often on longer-state logic, and each divergence costs more the longer the strategy stays in position. We find no robust evidence that volatility amplifies the loss, and errors are close to independent across strategies, so the risk is largely diversifiable. Frontier models still diverge silently on more than a quarter of tasks, and neither compilation, backtesting nor an LLM code review detects the divergence.
why: Critical: LLMs translating strategies to code with unexplained 100–2000bp shortfall

title: Artifact Integrity Does Not Imply Temporal Integrity: Evaluating Evidence-Bound Gates for Financial Research Agents
abstract: An unchanged financial research artifact can contain information disclosed after a historical cutoff, describe the wrong reporting period, or differ from the data a calculation subsequently uses. We separate byte integrity, conditional financial admissibility and consumption binding in a source-grounded calibration study. A fixed corpus of 80 quarterly filing records from ten issuers yields 73 usable records and 486 constructed financial-input cases. An independently coded SQLite baseline and a published validation engine match all constructed labels; disclosure-only filtering admits 121 of 194 known-invalid and all 146 insufficient-evidence cases. A separate experiment uses 48 distinct-duration pairs and three controlled consumption schedules. Reopening implementations consume out-of-contract facts in 96 of 144 cases; owner-contract-bound implementations consume none and retain every benign control. A revision-stage factorial diagnostic separates the two controls across four schedules: owner checking alone leaves 48 invalid consumptions per 192 cases, capture alone leaves 96, and their combination leaves zero. Both engines produce identical outcomes. Another 438 diagnostics check observation boundaries, equivalent timestamps and simultaneous missing evidence and violations. These dependent, engineered cases do not estimate production error rates. Fresh parsing corroborates listed facts but does not authenticate retained historical bytes; fabricated values and omitted later candidates can still pass. The contribution is an executable account of distinct financial-input obligations and their limits, without a claim of superiority over equivalent data engineering or evaluation of deployed autonomous agents. title: Do Domain Heuristics Help LLM Optimizers Calibrate an Agent-Based Limit Order Book?
abstract: Calibrating an agent-based limit-order-book (LOB) simulator is a prerequisite for credible simulated backtests of execution algorithms and market making, yet every evaluation is expensive, stochastic, and derivative-free. We study this calibration under a fixed budget of 50 simulator evaluations in an 11-dimensional parameter space. Six numerical baselines (Sobol sampling, a Treestructured Parzen Estimator (TPE), Bayesian Adaptive Direct Search (BADS), Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO), multiobjective TPE, and component-aware GP-BO) are compared with Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) driven by the large language model (LLM) Claude Sonnet 5, with and without frozen domain heuristics. We ask (1) whether an LLM proposal policy can allocate a fixed simulator budget competitively and (2) whether domain heuristics improve OPRO. A deterministic evaluator scores ticker-specific calibrations for five B3 equities with a standardized, grouped simulated-method-of-moments (SMM) loss over 29 moments of returns, spreads, imbalance, trade size, trade timing, and depth. All optimizers share one agent configuration, search domain, initial design, and budget, and selected parameters are evaluated on held-out dates. Averaged over five tickers and five repetitions, heuristic OPRO attains the lowest mean calibration endpoint (3.375) and held-out Test Book loss (4.575), against 5.002 and 5.973 for plain OPRO and 4.004 and 5.938 for component-aware GP-BO, the strongest numerical method. In this low-budget regime, OPRO is competitive with common black-box optimizers, and domain heuristics lower both its mean loss and its run-to-run variability.
why: LOB calibration with LLMs vs numeric methods, rigorous but proof-of-concept stage

title: The Three Faces of Fed Surprise: Rate-Path, Information and Tone Shocks in the Equity Cross-section
abstract: Every Federal Reserve announcement carries three surprises: a change in the expected policy path, a revision of the central bank's assessment of the economy, and the tone of the statement. We identify them as mutually orthogonal shocks on 219 announcements from 1994 to 2023, combining the Jarociński and Karadi (2020) sign-restriction decomposition, the Bauer and Swanson (2023b) orthogonalisation on the pre-announcement macro state and a Transformer classifier fine-tuned on the Shah et al. (2023) corpus, and trace each to the CRSP/Compustat cross-section, which is free of survivorship bias. The rate-path surprise dominates: a one-standard-deviation hawkish surprise lowers the market by about half a per cent, with the same sign in every regime and in nearly every rolling window, with a surprise built without equity prices, and on the announcements of 2024-2025. Its cross-section is the arithmetic of market exposure: the return to beta is what the CAPM implies from the market move, size adds little, and the balance-sheet characteristics that the literature associates with monetary transmission carry their usual signs on their own but none survives beta and size, in linear projections or in causal forests evaluated out of fold. The information surprise is small and positive. The tone surprise is small on average and its sign differs across periods, a pattern that bootstrapping the construction of the surprise, the level of the policy rate, the press conference and the announcements of 2024-2025 fail to confirm. Pre-registered predictions for 2024-2026 are reported as rejected, with a dated ledger of every deviation from the plan.
why: Fed announcement decomposition with Transformer classifier, solid but not LLM-focused

title: The Sharp End of AI Debt Market Evidence on Where the Off-Balance-Sheet Risk of the AI Build-Out Sits, 2016-2026
abstract: TThe Bank of England has warned that borrowing to build artificial intelligence leaves capital markets more exposed to the technology. It also acknowledges that the guarantees behind data-centre and chip financing make that risk hard to assess. This paper locates that risk from public data. The design comes from soil microbial ecology: every quantity is measured as an excess over a comparison group observed on the same days. Eighteen listed lenders to and investors in AI infrastructure are compared with 24 other financial stocks on the 35 days since 2024 when a basket of 46 AI supply-chain companies fell hardest. Significance comes from reshuffling the groups at random, under rules fixed in advance. The filings of the listed companies that contract with the main AI developers are then weighed against their market value. The debt has spread; the risk has not. Since 2024 the lenders have lagged other financial stocks by 0.54 percentage points a day when AI falls hardest. The gap was absent before 2024 and is concentrated in Blue Owl, Ares and Carlyle. The risk that OpenAI cannot meet its commitments sits with Oracle, CoreWeave and SoftBank, a concentration that S&P also cites in downgrading Oracle. Anthropic's commitments, of similar size, rest on groups able to absorb them. The telecoms boom shows such ties forming early and outlasting a crash. With OpenAI's listing deferred beyond 2026, the paper closes with four listing scenarios and the public measures that will tell them apart within a year.
why: AI infrastructure financing risk mapping, interesting macro data but not trading-focused

title: A Pre-Registered Test of Duplicated Inputs in Limit Order Book Encoders
abstract: Does handing a neural encoder a quantity it could compute from its other inputs change the representation it learns? We test this in a pre-registered comparison of input views of the limit order book, B6: NEST adds to the book's ladder 8 scalars that are exact, bit-identical functions of it and SUBST does not, so before the input transform the views differ in duplication, not information. Over 3 architectures, 3 objectives and 3 seeds on 5 spot pairs, each cell's NEST-to-SUBST similarity is compared with the similarity between seeds of one view. Per asset, B6-H1 (different representations) needs the shortfall below that seed ceiling to be permutation-significant in at least 6 of 9 cells, to average at least 0.1 in CKA and to be confirmed by mKNN; B6-H0 (the same) needs it to be neither significant nor that large; each needs 4 of 5 assets. B6-H1 is NOT SUPPORTED (0 of 5) and B6-H0 is NOT SUPPORTED (0 of 5): the significance clause holds on 5 of 5 assets and the margin clause on 0, and a shortfall larger than permutation noise and smaller than the size the design declared meaningful supports neither. As the design's reading stated before any figure existed, the significance clause asks little more than a positive shortfall, so the margin carries the evidence; on it alone, a reading that is not criterial, B6-H0 holds on 5 of 5 assets. Every figure is generated from the experiment's artifacts and checked by an independent verifier. AI disclosure. The author used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, throughout this work: to write and revise the code of the experiment's pipeline, the build and the verifier; to draft and revise the text of this paper; and to check both. The author directed the work, made its decisions, ran every computation, and reviewed all output, and takes full responsibility for the content.
why: Pre-registered null result on LOB encoder redundancy; rigorous but niche topic

title: Where Hindsight Credit Can Reside: A Signed-Capacity View of Token Updates in RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs), but sparse outcome rewards make token-level credit assignment difficult. We study token-level credit as a reward-conditioned shift from the behavior policy to a hindsight posterior. In autoregressive RLVR, this shift can be expressed through Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), which shows that token entropy upper-bounds possible hindsight credit. Entropy, however, indicates capacity rather than update direction, so we introduce the Four Quadrant Decomposition to separate updates by reward polarity and token entropy. Controlled interventions show that these two factors jointly shape token updates. Sustained reasoning gains concentrate in signed high-entropy quadrants, whereas low-entropy updates saturate quickly. Based on this analysis, we propose Hindsight-Aware Policy Optimization (HAPO), a sign-preserving modification to GRPO that performs capacity-guided advantage reallocation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks in two model settings show that HAPO achieves competitive performance among entropy-aware baselines.
why: LLM reasoning improvement via RLVR; general method, no financial application mentioned

title: Temporal Graph Neural Networks with Explainable AI for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: The increasing use of digital payments has created financial transaction networks that are large, interconnected, and continuously changing. This makes fraud detection more difficult than simply identifying unusual values in individual transaction records. Suspicious activity may be distributed across several accounts, appear through repeated interactions, or become visible only when the order and timing of transactions are considered. This paper presents a conceptual framework that combines Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for financial fraud detection and risk analysis. The proposed framework treats financial activity as a dynamic directed graph. Financial entities are represented as nodes and transactions are represented as time-stamped interactions. Graph learning is used to capture information from connected entities, while temporal modelling is intended to preserve changes in relationships and behavioural patterns over time. An explainability layer is proposed so that future model outputs can be examined through influential transaction attributes and, where appropriate, graph-level structures. PaySim is considered as a controlled synthetic dataset for future empirical validation. The methodology emphasizes data preparation, prevention of temporal leakage, chronological evaluation, comparison of transaction-level, static graph, and temporal graph approaches, and the use of Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC. The paper also discusses class imbalance, explanation limitations, privacy, fairness, robustness, scalability, and human oversight. This is a conceptual study; it does not report completed implementation or experimental performance. Its contribution is a structured research design that brings relational information, temporal behaviour, explainability, and responsible interpretation into one fraud-detection framework.
why: Fraud detection framework; conceptual only, no results or data presented

title: The Executive Second Brain: Retrieval-Augmented AI and Bias Mitigation in Marketing Leadership Under Volatility
abstract: Generative AI now sits alongside leaders as they write proposals, position offerings, and plan campaigns, and it is often touted as a cure for biased decisions. This article argues that, when used without forethought, it can do the opposite: it can return a leader's own bias wrapped in the guise of polished, confident strategy. Based on two and a half years of practitioner observation across AI solutions firms and client organizations in Bangladesh, reported as anonymized composite vignettes, the article presents a five-stage Sycophancy Loop: loaded framing, curated context, agreeable output, override and capitulation, and velocity without verification. In high power distance cultures, where employees do not dare to challenge the boss, AI is often the only advisor able to disagree, yet it is trained to agree. To escape the loop, the article introduces the Executive Second Brain, five practices that transform AI from a mirror into a challenger: inquiry framing, constraint-grounded retrieval, a standing license to dissent, an override protocol with a dissent log, and a verification gate. It concludes with testable propositions and an actionable checklist for leaders.
why: Off-topic: marketing leadership bias, not financial systems or LLM deployment

title: Artificial Intelligence in Banking: Transforming Risk Management Through Data-driven Innovation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), mostly based on supervised machine learning, is increasingly being implemented across commercial bank risk management areas. In compliance with the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this systematic umbrella review reports the search, selection, and synthesis process of AI-related literature in commercial banks' risk management. A total of 20 studies ranging from 2020 to 2026, published in Scopus and Web of Science databases, as well as in complementary searches, were included. The corpus includes 9 reviews and bibliometrics, and 11 empirical or theoretical papers. The former was evaluated with AMSTAR-2 and considered the context, while the latter received higher weights in synthesis. Benchmarking and review-level evidence suggests that machine learning can outperform rule-based and linear approaches in credit, fraud, and anti-money laundering. Still, the sole institutional comparison study is an uncontrolled mixed-methods study of five Bangladeshi institutions. The results of benchmarking and econometrics indicate that the complexity of a model is not necessarily linked to high precision and might lead to differences among various groups of borrowers. Systemic correlation, low level of explainability, legacy systems, and adaptive threats stay the unresolved barriers in all areas covered in this review. Time compression is identified as the common mechanism underlying the effect of AI on reduction of the gap between risk development and addressing it. This review outlines a layer of governance applicable to the EU AI Act, SR 11-7, and related regulatory tools. Generative AI and other emerging techniques are also discussed, although they are underrepresented in the literature. Banks should pair algorithmic adoption with fairness testing, explainability infrastructure, and documented human oversight.
why: Systematic review/survey: explicitly rejected category, synthesis of existing work

title: THE PRIMARY ASSUMPTION IN ASSET PRICING FINANCE THEORY IS WRONG! AN AGENTIC SOLUTION?
abstract: This paper addresses and seeks to resolve a tension between investment theory and practice. Bad theories can lead to bad practice with severe economic consequences (Case A); not so when bad theory is ignored by practitioners who adopt best practices (Case B). We explore both cases, and two others, to try to improve theory and practice. The argument rests on the primary assumption made in almost all asset pricing theories, that "risk averse investors maximize the expected utility of wealth (or MEUAW)". This assumption fails three scientific/basic tests.
why: Theory position paper: claims asset pricing assumption wrong, vague solution, incomplete abstract

title: Markdown Pricing When Shoppers Delegate to AI Agents
abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate purchases to AI shopping agents that track prices at no cost. An agent removes a shopper's inattention, but it does not remove her impatience. We study how a seller should set its markdown policy when consumers differ both in whether they shop through an agent and in whether they are willing to wait. Agents have two effects. Patient agent users wait for the sale, which undermines the markdown. Impatient agent users still buy at the full price when it is acceptable, but now never miss the sale, which makes the markdown a sharper tool for price discrimination. Seller profit depends on the market only through two statistics, the mass of non-strategic consumers who see the sale and the mass of patient agent users. The seller either accommodates agents by keeping a deep markdown and raising both prices, or compresses the markdown so that high-valuation agents buy early, and the switch between the two can be abrupt. A larger impatient share delays the switch and, beyond a point, removes it entirely. Agents lower the seller's profit unless the impatient share exceeds a threshold, above which full adoption raises profit. Human shoppers lose throughout the accommodation regime in every case we compute, including when agents raise the seller's profit. Identification of agent traffic restores the all-human markdown for humans, and a seller that can block agents prefers to do so exactly when the impatient share is below the profit threshold. When adoption is costly, patient consumers adopt first, adoption can stall where sellers abandon their markdowns, and the consumers who adopt are the ones whose adoption lowers total welfare.
why: Off-topic: retail e-commerce pricing, not financial markets or trading

title: Non-Custodial Compliance for Regulated Markets Private Eligibility and Holder-Controlled Participation
abstract: In regulated capital markets, the design of qualification checks shapes who controls access to financial relationships and what investors must disclose. When certification is coupled to operator-controlled recognition, investors who meet the rules may still require additional approval to use another account or compatible service. We present non-custodial compliance, an architecture that separates authoritative certification from the private, holder-controlled exercise of accepted qualification. Institutions establish facts and publish status; holders present evidence and authorize financial instructions; applications enforce their rules against the relevant participants and actual financial effects. Qualification remains independent of the accepting asset, application and execution account. A matched implementation evaluates enforcement, disclosure and institutional cooperation together. Its private, independent profile preserves the tested participant and financial rules without an additional operator-controlled registration step or individualized institutional permit, while concealing the credential fields disclosed by the public comparison profile. Within a shared reserve, a restriction blocks the affected participant's governed actions while another qualified participant redeems under unchanged reserve controls. A capable institutional alternative also preserves its permit through evidence refresh, but retains an initial approval requirement. Failure experiments demonstrate why individually valid credentials and approvals are insufficient when their participant or financial-effect bindings disagree. The security argument establishes conditions under which refreshed evidence preserves the holder's approved financial authority. Accounts, financial effects and position linkage remain public. The resulting architecture allows compatible services to verify accepted qualification and investor consent without requiring another operator's individualized approval of participation. title: The Cost of Constant Change: Expatriate Rotation and the Erosion of Psychological Safety in a Chinese Fintech's Nigerian Subsidiary
abstract: This paper examines an underexamined source of instability facing Chinese enterprises operating in West Africa: not external market volatility, but the frequency with which the Chinese expatriate managers leading local operations are rotated. Using a detailed single-employee case from a Chinese-invested fintech's Nigerian subsidiary — an employee who, after working under three managers in eight months, described losing the ability to predict what his role required, and who subsequently left the company — this paper develops a two-stage psychological mechanism linking rotation frequency to local employee withdrawal. Drawing on Uncertainty Reduction Theory (Berger & Calabrese, 1975) and Psychological Safety (Edmondson, 1999), we propose that high-frequency managerial rotation increases employees' perceived uncertainty about role expectations, which in turn suppresses their psychological safety and produces downstream withdrawal behaviors — turnover, internal transfer-seeking, and reduced discretionary effort. We further propose that transparent, procedurally fair communication around each transition moderates this relationship, offering organizations a lower-cost lever where rotation frequency itself cannot easily be reduced. The paper is conceptual and illustrative rather than statistically confirmatory, grounded in a single case supplemented by department-level organizational data spanning thirteen departments over a fifteen-month window — data that shows the proposed pattern clearly among contract staff but not among regular employees, an asymmetry the paper interprets rather than smooths over. It contributes to the literature on Chinese enterprises' overseas human resource management by reframing a portion of "instability" as internally generated and organizationally addressable, and offers concrete, low-cost recommendations — standardized transition communication, staggered rotation scheduling, and routine tracking of rotation frequency as an HR indicator — for practice. AI disclosure: The author used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with structuring the manuscript, drafting and editing text, and checking references. The research question, case observations, organizational data, and interpretive judgments are the author's own; all content was reviewed and revised by the author, who takes full responsibility for the final text.
